title: Germs: how illness travels from person to person

summary.text: You can catch a cold from someone you never touched. Germs are the few microbes that can make us ill, and they cannot walk or fly from one person to the next. They ride on hands, on the things hands touch, in the drops of a cough, in water and food, and on flies and mosquitoes. Once inside a body, a few germs can multiply into millions, and that is an infection. An illness spreads along a chain, from the ill person, to a ride, to the next person. Breaking one link of that chain stops the illness there.
summary.art: A chain of pictures joined by dotted arrows: a girl coughing into her hand, the hand on a door handle, a second hand on the same handle, that hand near a boy's mouth, with a big pair of scissors cutting the chain at the door handle.

intro.hook: Think of the main door of your flat. Who touched its handle today? Count everyone, and then think about who touched the things they touched.
intro.text: Germs are far too small to see, and they have no legs or wings to cross a room. Yet a cold can go round a whole family in a week, and a tummy bug can go round a whole school. So how does a germ get from one person to another? In this unit you follow the trail with glitter, which you can see, and find out how far one hand can reach.
intro.art: The inside of a flat's main door, with many small, different hands drawn faintly around the handle, as if everyone who touched it that day left a mark.

outcomes: I can say what germs are: the few bacteria, viruses and other microbes that can make us ill.
I can name the ways germs travel: on hands, on things we touch, in cough and sneeze drops, in water and food, and on flies and mosquitoes.
I can explain, using the Glitter Trail experiment, how germs reach people who never touched the ill person.
I can say what an infection is: germs getting inside the body and multiplying.
I can choose where to break a chain of illness, and say why that works.
I can tell how John Snow found that cholera came from one water pump, and not from bad air.

terms.meaning: A living being too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria and many fungi are microbes.
terms.example: The bacteria that turn milk into curd are microbes.
terms.art: A bowl of curd with a zoomed-in circle showing tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: A microbe or virus that can make people, animals or plants ill. Only a few kinds of microbe are germs.
terms.example: The virus that gives you a cold is a germ. The bacteria in curd are not.
terms.art: Many small friendly-looking microbes, with just two of them circled in red and labelled 'germ'.

terms.meaning: Living beings made of just one tiny cell. One of them is called a bacterium. Most are harmless or helpful, and a few cause illness.
terms.example: Cholera is caused by a bacterium that lives in dirty water.
terms.art: A few rod-shaped and round bacteria, each a single cell, some with a long whip-like tail.

terms.meaning: Germs much smaller than bacteria. Viruses can make copies of themselves only inside the cells of another living being.
terms.example: Colds, flu and chickenpox are caused by viruses.
terms.art: A tiny round virus landing on a much bigger cell, drawn to scale beside a bacterium.

terms.meaning: When germs get inside a body and multiply there.
terms.example: A cut that turns red and sore may have an infection.
terms.art: A small cut on a knee, with a zoom showing a few germs inside becoming many.

terms.meaning: To grow in number. Bacteria multiply by splitting in two, again and again.
terms.art: One bacterium splitting into two, then four, then eight, in a row of pictures.

terms.meaning: A sign in your body that you are ill, such as a fever, a cough, a runny nose or loose motions.
terms.example: Sneezing and a blocked nose are symptoms of a cold.
terms.art: A girl with a tissue and a blocked nose, with small labels pointing to a sneeze and a warm forehead.

terms.meaning: An illness is contagious when it can pass from one person to another.
terms.example: Chickenpox is very contagious. A broken bone is not contagious at all.
terms.art: Two children side by side, one with chickenpox spots and a dotted arrow towards the other, and one with a leg in plaster and no arrow.

terms.meaning: Tiny drops of spit and mucus that fly out when we cough, sneeze, talk or sing. They can carry germs.
terms.example: A sneeze can spray droplets across a room.
terms.art: A side view of a sneeze, with a spray of tiny drops flying out and falling to the floor.

terms.meaning: When many people in one place fall ill with the same illness at around the same time.
terms.example: In 1854, a cholera outbreak in one part of London killed more than 500 people in ten days.
terms.art: A street map of a few blocks with many dots on houses close to one water pump.

terms.meaning: An illness caused by bacteria in dirty water or food. It gives very watery loose motions, so the body quickly loses water.
terms.example: Clean drinking water and toilets stop cholera spreading.
terms.art: A clean steel pot of boiled water with a lid, next to a muddy open well, crossed out.

terms.meaning: A medicine that kills bacteria, or stops them multiplying. Antibiotics do not work on viruses.
terms.example: A doctor may give an antibiotic for a bacterial throat infection, but not for a cold, which is a virus.
terms.art: A strip of tablets beside a picture of a bacterium with a tick and a virus with a cross.

explanations.definition: Germs are the bacteria, viruses, fungi and other tiny living beings that can cause illness. Only a small share of all microbes are germs.
explanations.description: Microbes live almost everywhere: in soil, in water, in curd, and all over and inside you. Your body carries about as many bacteria as there are cells of your own. Nearly all of them do you no harm, and many help you, for example by breaking down food in your gut. A few kinds can make you ill. Those are the ones we call germs. Bacteria are single living cells. Viruses are much smaller, and can make copies of themselves only inside someone else's cells. Most colds, flu, chickenpox and measles are caused by viruses. Cholera, typhoid and many tummy upsets are caused by bacteria. Ringworm, an itchy round rash, is caused by a fungus.
examples: The bacteria in curd are microbes, but not germs.
The virus that causes a cold is a germ.
Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not a worm.
explanations.art: A big circle labelled 'all microbes', mostly filled with harmless ones in soil, curd and on skin, with a small slice of it shaded and labelled 'germs'.
explanations.context: This card explains what a germ is, and why most microbes are not germs.

explanations.concept: A germ's own problem: getting to a new body
explanations.definition: Germs live by multiplying. To keep going, their copies must get out of one body and into another.
explanations.description: Think about life from the side of cold viruses. They can only make copies inside the cells of a nose or throat. Within about a week, the body's defences clear them out. So cold viruses who stay in one nose come to an end. Their family goes on only if some copies reach a new nose first. A runny nose and sneezes help them do that, because they carry copies out of the body. Cholera bacteria leave the body in loose motions, and reach a new person if that water is drunk. Each kind of germ has a way out of one body and into the next. Every illness that spreads is a germ travelling this way.
examples: A cold virus travels out in a sneeze, or on a hand that wiped a nose.
Cholera bacteria travel out in loose motions, and reach a new person through drinking water.
The dengue virus travels from one person's blood to another's inside a mosquito.
explanations.art: A cold virus drawn as a tiny round being in a nose, with an arrow out on a sneeze drop and into a second nose across the room.
explanations.context: This card looks at germs from their own side: why they must keep moving from one body to the next.

explanations.definition: Germs travel on hands, on things that hands touch, in droplets from coughs and sneezes, in water and food, and on insects.
explanations.description: Many bacteria can swim, but only a tiny distance. Viruses cannot move on their own at all. So germs need a ride. The most common ride is a hand. A hand wipes a nose, then touches a door handle, a lift button, a TV remote or a steel tumbler. The next hand picks the germs up from there, and carries them to an eye, a nose or a mouth. In this way germs can pass through several hands and things before they reach a new person. Coughs and sneezes spray droplets that fly through the air and land on people and things nearby. Dirty water and uncovered food carry germs into the stomach. Flies walk on rubbish, then on food. Some mosquitoes carry the germs of dengue and malaria from one person's blood to another's.
examples: A boy sneezes into his hand and opens the fridge. His sister opens the fridge an hour later and then eats a biscuit.
A sneeze into the air sprays droplets onto everyone at the table.
A fly walks on a rubbish heap and then on an open plate of jalebis.
explanations.art: Five small pictures in a ring around a child: a hand, a door handle, a sneeze, a glass of water, a fly, each with a dotted arrow pointing to the child's mouth or nose.
explanations.context: This card lists the rides germs take from one person to another. The Glitter Trail experiment shows one of them: hands and the things hands touch.

explanations.definition: An infection is when germs get inside the body and multiply there.
explanations.description: Germs land on our skin all the time. Skin with no cuts keeps most of them out. They get in mostly through the soft, wet linings of the eyes, nose and mouth, and through cuts. Inside, they find warmth, water and food, so they multiply. In the best conditions, some bacteria can split in two about every 20 minutes. One bacterium can then become thousands in a few hours. A virus gets inside a cell and makes the cell build many new copies of the virus. The illness you feel is partly the germs' work and partly your body fighting back. A fever, a runny nose and tiredness are mostly signs of your body's fight. That is why you may feel well for a day or two after catching a germ, before the symptoms start.
examples: A cold usually starts one to three days after the virus gets into your nose.
A dirty cut can turn red, warm and sore as bacteria multiply in the cut.
Rice left warm on the stove all day can grow enough bacteria to cause a tummy upset.
explanations.art: Three panels: a few germs landing on a nose, the same germs multiplying inside, and a girl in bed with a fever two days later.
explanations.context: This card explains the difference between germs landing on you and an infection.

explanations.concept: Why one person gets ill and another does not
explanations.definition: Whether a germ makes you ill depends on how many germs reach you, where they get in, and how ready your body's defences are.
explanations.description: Two children can sit with the same ill friend, and only one of them catches the cold. A few germs are often cleared out before they can multiply. Many germs at once are harder to clear. Germs on your hand do nothing until they reach your eye, nose or mouth. A body that has met a germ before, or has had a vaccine for that germ, often clears that germ quickly. Sleep and good food help the defences too. So spreading is a matter of chance, and each way we block the germs makes the chance smaller. How the body fights germs is in the unit on the immune system.
examples: A child who washes before eating gives the germs on their hand less chance to reach their mouth.
A child who has had the measles vaccine is very unlikely to catch measles, even in an outbreak.
In the Handshake Chain experiment, glitter passes from hand to hand. The hands further down the chain get fewer specks, just as fewer germs reach people further along a chain.
explanations.art: Two children at a table with an ill friend: one wiping her hands on a cloth and the other putting a hand to his mouth, with a few germs on each hand.
explanations.context: This card explains why not everyone who meets a germ gets ill.

explanations.definition: Germs spread along a chain of links. Breaking any one link stops that chain.
explanations.description: Every germ trail has links: the ill person, the way out (a sneeze, a hand), the ride (a handle, the air, water), the way in (a mouth, a nose), and the next person. You only need to break one. Coughing into your elbow keeps germs off your hands, so they never reach the door handle. Washing hands before eating breaks the link from hand to mouth. Boiling or filtering drinking water breaks the water link. Covering food breaks the fly link. Staying home when you are ill keeps the first link away from everyone else. Each habit is small, but it stops every trail that would have passed through that link.
examples: A girl with a cough coughs into her elbow, so her hands stay clean for the lift button.
A family boils its drinking water, so germs in the tank water never reach their stomachs.
A girl with flu stays home, so her classmates never meet her germs.
explanations.art: A paper chain of five links labelled 'ill person', 'way out', 'ride', 'way in', 'next person', with one link cut open by scissors.
explanations.context: This card explains why one small habit can stop a germ from reaching many people.

explanations.concept: Do colds spread more by hands or through the air?
explanations.description: Scientists have argued about this for fifty years, and the answer may be different for different germs. Colds are a good example. Some careful tests found that colds spread mostly on hands, and other careful tests found that they spread mostly through the air. Each side had real evidence, so both habits matter: wash your hands, and cover coughs and sneezes.
examples: In the 1970s, a team in the United States found cold viruses on the hands of people with colds, and on things they had touched.

In the 1980s, another team made men with colds play cards for hours with healthy men. Some healthy men wore stiff collars or arm braces so they could not touch their faces, and many of them still caught colds.

perspectives.who: Jack Gwaltney and Owen Hendley, University of Virginia, 1970s
perspectives.explanation: They found cold viruses on the hands of people with colds. When healthy people touched those hands and then their own eyes or nose, many caught the cold. So they said hands are the main way colds spread.

perspectives.who: Elliot Dick and his team, University of Wisconsin, 1987
perspectives.explanation: In their card-playing tests, healthy men who could not touch their faces still caught colds from the ill players. So they said colds spread mostly through the air, in tiny droplets breathed out.
Colds can spread both ways, and which way matters more may depend on the place and the virus. So it is worth breaking both links.

explanations.art: A card table with four men playing cards, one sneezing, and two others wearing stiff collars that stop their hands reaching their faces.
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument between scientists: do colds travel more on hands or in the air?

agreed.text: Many illnesses are caused by germs: tiny bacteria, viruses, fungi and other small living beings.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can see the germs under microscopes, grow many of them in the lab, and show that they cause the same illness again and again.

agreed.text: Most microbes are harmless or helpful. Only a few kinds are germs.
agreed.evidence: Every healthy person carries many trillions of bacteria. Curd, idli batter and soil are full of microbes that do us no harm.

agreed.text: Germs spread on hands and touched things, in cough and sneeze droplets, in water and food, and through some insects.
agreed.evidence: Germs have been found on hands, door handles and phones, in dirty water and in mosquitoes. Illness falls when these paths are blocked.

agreed.text: Washing hands with soap and water cuts the spread of tummy upsets and coughs.
agreed.evidence: A large study in Karachi, in Pakistan, gave families soap and showed them how to wash. Their children had about half as much diarrhoea and chest infection as children in families who were not given soap.

agreed.text: Clean drinking water and toilets stop cholera and typhoid spreading.
agreed.evidence: London had its last big cholera outbreak in 1866, after it built new sewers and began to clean its drinking water. Since then, many other cities have seen cholera stop once clean water and drains arrived.

agreed.text: Antibiotics kill bacteria but do nothing to viruses.
agreed.evidence: Antibiotics work by attacking parts that only bacteria have. Viruses do not have those parts. Tests show antibiotics do not make colds better.

challenging.claim: You can only catch a germ from someone you touch or sit next to.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: We often catch a cold just after sitting beside someone with one, so the closeness seems to be the cause.
challenging.against: Germs ride on things. In the Glitter Trail experiment, one person, the carrier, has glitter on their hand. People who never touched the carrier still had glitter on their hands, from the door handle and the remote. John Snow found people who caught cholera far from the outbreak, because they drank water from the same pump.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that germs pass only between people who touch.

challenging.claim: If you feel well, you cannot pass on a germ.
challenging.for: When we feel well, there is no cough or runny nose to spread anything.
challenging.against: With many illnesses, such as flu and colds, people pass on germs a day or so before they feel ill. Some people carry germs, such as typhoid bacteria, without ever feeling ill. That is why washing matters even on a day you feel fine.
challenging.context: This card is about whether only ill-looking people can spread germs.

challenging.claim: An antibiotic will cure a cold faster.
challenging.who: A common belief. Many people ask doctors for antibiotics for a cold.
challenging.for: Antibiotics work very well against some infections, so it seems they should help with any illness.
challenging.against: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work only on bacteria. Taking antibiotics when they are not needed helps bacteria become resistant, which means the medicine no longer kills them. Then the medicine does not work when it is really needed.
challenging.context: This card is about whether antibiotics help with a cold.

challenging.claim: Everyone who meets a germ gets ill.
challenging.for: Germs cause illness, so it seems any contact should make you ill.
challenging.against: Your skin, nose, stomach and immune system clear out most germs before they can multiply. How many germs reach you, and whether your body has met them before, both matter. That is why only some people in a family catch the same cold.
challenging.context: This card is about whether meeting a germ always makes you ill.

big_questions.q: In the Handshake Chain, the glitter got less with each hand it passed through. Do germs get fewer in the same way along a chain?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to the glitter on each hand and each handle. Real germs can also die on dry surfaces, or multiply in warm, wet food.

big_questions.q: A cold virus can only make copies inside someone's cells. Is a virus alive?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a living thing does: eats, grows, makes copies. Scientists still argue about viruses.

big_questions.q: Why do you think some germs make us cough and sneeze, while others give us loose motions?
big_questions.hint: Think about how each germ gets out of one body and into the next.

big_questions.q: A family on the floor above you never meets you, yet you all share the lift button. How many people are you joined to by the things you touch?
big_questions.hint: Think of the door handles, buttons, coins and railings you touch in one day, and who else touches them.

big_questions.q: When you stay home with a cold, who are you protecting? Can you ever know?
big_questions.hint: Think about a chain that never starts. Nobody can count the illnesses that did not happen.

big_questions.q: Germs are living beings trying to keep their family going, as all living beings do. How should we think about killing them with medicines?
big_questions.hint: Think about how a farmer thinks about pests, and how the Jains think about tiny beings.

story.title: Paati's Pongal Pot
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is true: colds spread on hands and touched things as well as through the air, people can pass on a cold before they feel ill, and coughing into the elbow keeps germs off the hands.
text: Three days before Pongal, Kavya woke up with a blocked nose and a scratchy throat. She sneezed so hard that her plait swung round and hit her ear.
"Oh no," said Amma from the kitchen door. "A cold. And Paati arrives from Tiruchi tomorrow."

Paati was Kavya's grandmother. She was seventy-four, and last winter a cold had turned into a bad cough that kept her in bed for three weeks. This year she was coming to their flat in Coimbatore to make the Pongal rice with Kavya, in the big brass pot on the balcony, the way they did every year.
"I don't understand," said Kavya, blowing her nose. "Nandini had a cold at school. But I stayed far away from her. I didn't even sit at her table."
Appa looked up from his newspaper. "You must have stood next to someone else, then. Colds come from people breathing on you."
Kavya frowned. That was part of it, she knew. But she had been careful. She sat on her bed and thought back over the school day, the way a detective goes over a case.

Nandini had sat by the window. Kavya had sat by the door. But at lunch, they had both used the tap by the water filter. Nandini had pressed the filter button with her hand, and Kavya had pressed it too, to fill her bottle. In art, everyone had used the same box of crayons. And the lift in their building had one button for the fourth floor, and Nandini lived on the fourth floor too.
"Appa," said Kavya slowly. "I think the cold came to me on a button."

Appa laughed, but Amma did not. Amma was a nurse at the health centre near the bus stand. "That can happen," she said. "Cold germs can stay alive on a hard button for a few hours. Nandini wipes her nose, presses the button, and the germs wait there. Then your finger comes along. Later, you rub your eye or bite your nail, and the germs are in."
"So I caught Nandini's cold without ever touching Nandini," said Kavya.
"Quite likely," said Amma. "Or in the air. Nobody can be sure which way it came. But now the question is how to keep it from Paati."

Kavya thought about that all evening. If her cold had come along a chain of hands and buttons, then she could break the chain before it reached Paati. She made a list on the back of an old calendar page.

Number one: sneeze and cough into my elbow, not my hand. Then my hands stay clean for door handles. Number two: my own steel tumbler, with a sticker on it, that nobody else uses. Number three: wash my hands with soap after blowing my nose, every single time. Number four: no hugging Paati until my cold has gone, even though I really want to.
She read the list to Appa. "You have to do it too," she told him. "You sneeze into your hand all the time. Then you pick up the TV remote."
Appa opened his mouth to argue, then closed it again. "Fine," he said. "Elbow."
Her little brother Arjun was six, and he did not like lists. "Why do I have to?" he said. "I'm not ill."
"You might be ill tomorrow and not know it yet," said Kavya. "Amma says you can pass a cold on before you feel it."

Paati came the next day with a bag of fresh turmeric plants and a basket of sugarcane. Kavya waved to her from across the room and pointed to her own nose. "Cold," she said. "No hugs until it goes. But I'm washing my hands like a doctor."
Paati laughed. "Then you can still stir the pot," she said. "Wash first, and stir from the side, away from my face."

On Pongal morning, Kavya washed her hands with soap at the balcony tap, slowly, counting to twenty. She held the long ladle and stirred the rice and milk while Paati added jaggery. When the milk rose and spilled over the edge of the pot, everyone shouted "Pongalo Pongal!" Kavya shouted it into her elbow, just in case.
Two days later, Kavya's cold was better. Paati was still well.
But Arjun woke up sneezing.
"I did my list!" said Kavya. "Well, nearly. Arjun, did you wipe your nose on your hand?"
Arjun looked at his shoes. "Only once. And then I played with the remote."
Kavya sighed. Then she took a sticker and wrote a big A on it, for Arjun's own tumbler. "Right," she said. "New list. Paati is still here for four more days."
Paati went home to Tiruchi a week later, without a cough. On the phone that night she told Kavya, "You looked after me without touching me once. That is a clever kind of care."
story.epiphany: For the parent: a cold travels along a chain of people, hands and things, and also through the air. Kavya could not see the germs, but she could see the links: the button, the tumbler, the remote, the sneeze into a hand. Breaking a link protects people further along the chain, even people we never touch.
ask: How did Kavya work out that her cold might have come on a button?
Why did Kavya sneeze into her elbow instead of her hand?
Why did Arjun have to follow the list even though he was not ill?
Paati stayed well, but Arjun caught the cold. Which rule on Kavya's list did Arjun not follow?
What would you put on a list to keep someone at home well?

games.title: Germ Chain: build and break a chain
games.context: This is a card game. One player builds germ chains from an ill person to a next person. The other player breaks them with STOP cards.

printables.title: 22 chain cards to cut out (5 kinds of link)
items: ILL PERSON: Meenakshi has a cold.
ILL PERSON: Farhan has a tummy bug.
ILL PERSON: Thatha has an eye infection.
WAY OUT: the ill person sneezes into a hand.
WAY OUT: the ill person does not wash after the toilet.
WAY OUT: the ill person coughs into the air.
WAY OUT: the ill person wipes the nose with a hand.
RIDE: an uncovered plate of dhokla.
WAY IN: the next person rubs the eyes.
WAY IN: the next person eats a biscuit without washing the hands.
WAY IN: the next person bites the nails.
WAY IN: the next person picks the nose.

printables.title: 8 STOP cards to cut out
items: STOP: coughs or sneezes into the elbow. Breaks a WAY OUT link of sneezing into a hand or coughing into the air.
STOP: washes the hands with soap after the toilet or after wiping the nose. Breaks a WAY OUT link.
STOP: everyone has their own tumbler. Breaks the tumbler RIDE.
STOP: covers the food with a plate. Breaks the food RIDE.
STOP: wipes the handle, the button and the remote with soapy water. Breaks a handle, button or remote RIDE.
STOP: opens a window wide. Breaks the droplets RIDE.
STOP: washes the hands with soap before eating or touching the face. Breaks a WAY IN link.
STOP: stays home until well. Breaks an ILL PERSON link.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Chains that reached a next person: ____
Which link was broken most often? ____

rules: With 2 players, one is the Germ and one is the Chain Breaker. With 3 or 4 players, one is the Germ and the others are Chain Breakers who decide together.

Sort the 22 chain cards into five piles by kind and shuffle each pile. The Germ turns over the top card of each pile and lays them in a row: ILL PERSON, WAY OUT, RIDE, WAY IN, NEXT PERSON. Read the row aloud as one story. If the story makes no sense at all, swap one card for the next card in its pile.
The Chain Breakers hold the 8 STOP cards. They may play one STOP card on any link it fits.
If a STOP card breaks a link, the chain is broken. The Chain Breakers score 1 point and say why the germ is stuck.
If no STOP card fits, the germ reaches the next person. The Germ scores 1 point.
Each STOP card can be used only once while the same player is the Germ. Put the chain cards back and shuffle after each round.

Play 6 rounds with 2 or 3 players, or 8 rounds with 4. With 2 players, swap roles after 3 rounds. With more players, a new player becomes the Germ after every round. Take back all 8 STOP cards whenever the Germ changes. The highest score wins, and a tie is shared.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Sort the chain cards into the five kinds. 3. Give the STOP cards to the Chain Breaker.
flow.say: Germs cannot walk. They need a chain of links to get from one person to the next. You will build chains, and I will try to break them.
flow.kid: You are the Germ. Build a chain with one card of each kind: ill person, way out, ride, way in, next person.
flow.context: This is the first step of Germ Chain, a card game about how germs travel and how to stop them.

flow.do: Play one practice round. Read the chain aloud as a story.
flow.say: Read your chain as a story. Meenakshi has a cold. She sneezes into her hand. She presses the lift button. Then Lakshmi presses the same button and rubs her eyes. Which STOP card would break it?
flow.kid: Read your chain like a story. Which STOP card could break it?

check.q: Meenakshi sneezes into her hand, then presses the lift button. Which habit breaks this chain?
check.why: Sneezing into her elbow keeps the germs off her hand, so they never get onto the button. Water and a sweater are good for her, but they do not stop germs travelling.

flow.do: Play 6 rounds (8 with four players), changing the Germ as the rules say. After each round, the Chain Breaker says which link they broke and why.
flow.say: Which link did you break? Why does that stop the germ? Could another STOP card have worked too?
flow.kid: Play the rounds. Say which link you broke, and why.

ask.q: Was there a chain you could break in two places?
good: Yes. A sneeze chain can be broken at the way out with the elbow, at the ride by wiping the handle, or at the way in by washing hands.
The food chain. Cover the food (the ride), or wash hands before eating (the way in).

flow.do: Count the points. Look at which kind of STOP card was used most.
flow.say: Which link did we break most often? Which one is easiest to break in our own home?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which link is easiest to break at home?
flow.think: Is there a link in our home that nobody is breaking yet?

Stop, because water washes germs away

experiments.title: The Glitter Trail: can germs reach someone you never touched?
experiments.question: If one person has pretend germs on their hand, who in the home ends up with them? Do people who never touched that person get them too? And does a cough into the elbow change that?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. The carrier is the person with glitter on their hand. After 10 minutes, will anyone who did not touch the carrier have glitter on their hands? Who will have the most? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, the carrier touches the same list of things in both rounds, in the same order, and the same people take part. Use one pinch of glitter each time. Only one thing changes: in round 1 the glitter is on the carrier's palm, and in round 2 it is on the inside of their elbow.
results_table: Did they touch the carrier? (yes or no)
Glitter in round 1 (palm): none, a few specks, lots
Glitter in round 2 (elbow): none, a few specks, lots

materials.item: a small tube of glitter from a stationery shop, about one spoon. No glitter? Use a pinch of kumkum or rangoli colour instead.
a few drops of coconut oil or any cooking oil
a torch, or a phone torch
5 things to touch: the main door handle, the fridge handle, the TV remote, an empty steel tumbler and a pencil
at least one other person at home to be the helper (more are welcome)
soap, water and an old cloth for cleaning up

experiments.safety: Keep glitter away from eyes and mouth. Never put glitter on food, plates or anything that goes in the mouth. Use an empty tumbler for the test and wash it afterwards. At the end, a grown-up wipes up all the glitter with a damp cloth and shakes the cloth into the dustbin, not down the drain, because glitter is plastic. If you use kumkum or rangoli colour instead of glitter, keep it off sofas and clothes, because it can stain light cloth.

schedule.what: Round 1: put glitter on the carrier's palm. The carrier touches the things on the touch list, then you check everyone's hands with a torch. Wash and clean up. Round 2: put glitter on the carrier's elbow, do the same touch list, and check again.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw your home as a map, with each person and each thing as a dot. Draw an arrow for every way the glitter travelled.

flow.do: 1. Choose your child as the carrier and another person as the helper. 2. Read the touch list aloud together: main door, fridge, remote, steel tumbler, pencil. 3. Check everyone's hands with the torch: there should be no glitter yet. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Real germs are too small to see. Today glitter is our pretend germ, and you are the ill person carrying the glitter. Here is the touch list. Will anyone who never touches you end up with glitter? Who will have the most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Glitter is your pretend germ. You are the carrier. Guess who will get glitter. Why?

ask.q: Who do you think will get the most glitter, and why?
good: The person I hold hands with, because they touch me straight away.
Whoever touches the door handle first after me.

flow.parent: Write the guess down. Do not say what you expect. Any reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Glitter Trail. You put glitter on one person's hand as pretend germs, and follow where it goes in your home.

flow.do: 1. Rub two drops of oil on your child's right palm. 2. Sprinkle one pinch of glitter on it. 3. Your child rubs both palms together once.
flow.say: Skin has its own thin layer of oil, and germs sit in that layer. The drops of oil make the glitter stick to your hand the way germs do.
flow.kid: Rub two drops of oil on your right palm. Add a pinch of glitter. Rub your hands together once.
flow.parent: Use a small pinch, about as much as fits on the tip of a teaspoon. Too much glitter falls everywhere and makes the trail hard to read.

flow.do: The carrier does the touch list: 1. Open and close the main door. 2. Open and close the fridge. 3. Press three buttons on the remote. 4. Pick up the steel tumbler and put it down. 5. Put the pencil down on the table. Nobody touches the carrier.
flow.say: Now go through the list, just as you would on a normal day. Remember, you must not touch anyone else.
flow.kid: Touch each thing on the list: door, fridge, remote, tumbler, pencil. Don't touch anyone!

flow.do: Now the helper does their part. 1. Pick up the pencil and write a word. 2. Open the fridge. 3. Open and close the main door. 4. Pick up the remote and the steel tumbler. Anyone else at home can do the same, one after another.
flow.say: Now the helper does what they usually do. The helper never went near the carrier.
flow.kid: Now the helper uses the pencil, fridge, door, remote and tumbler. Watch carefully.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the light or close the curtain. 2. Shine the torch across each person's palms and each thing. 3. Look for glitter sparkling in the beam. 4. Score each one: none, a few specks, or lots.
flow.say: Shine the torch at a low angle, almost flat. Glitter flashes when the light hits it. Who has glitter? Did the helper get any?
flow.kid: Shine the torch across each hand. Do you see sparkles? Score them.

ask.q: How did glitter get onto the helper's hands?
good: From the door handle and the remote, which the carrier touched first.
It rode on the things.

check.q: The helper never touched the carrier, but has glitter on a hand. Where did it come from?
options: From the things the carrier touched first, like the door handle
It flew through the air by itself
It was already on their hand
check.why: The glitter rode from the carrier's hand to the handle and the remote, and from there to the next hand. Picking 'flew by itself' would mean glitter moves on its own. It cannot, and neither can most germs. Picking 'already there' is worth checking: that is why we look at everyone's hands before we start.

flow.do: 1. Everyone washes hands well with soap. 2. Wipe the door, fridge, remote, tumbler and pencil with a damp soapy cloth. 3. Check with the torch that the glitter has gone.
flow.say: Before round 2, everything must be clean, or old glitter will spoil the test.
flow.kid: Everyone washes their hands with soap. Wipe the things too. Check with the torch.

flow.do: Round 2: 1. Put the oil and the same pinch of glitter on the inside of the carrier's elbow. 2. Do exactly the same touch list. 3. The helper does their part again. 4. Check with the torch and score.
flow.say: This time the glitter is on your elbow, as if you had coughed into it. Everything else stays the same. What do you think will change? Why?
flow.kid: Now glitter goes on your elbow, like a cough. Same touch list. What changes?
flow.parent: Usually only a few specks, or none, reach the things and the others' hands. If you see some, look at where they are: often on a sleeve or a tabletop the elbow brushed.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think happened? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened that way?
flow.kid: Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What did round 2 show about coughing into your elbow?
good: Much less glitter got onto the things, so less reached the others.
The elbow does not touch door handles.

flow.think: Which thing in our home do the most hands touch in a day?

experiments.context: In this experiment you use glitter as pretend germs and follow its trail round your home, from one person's hand to things and other people.

experiments.title: The Handshake Chain: do germs get fewer along a chain?
experiments.question: When glitter passes from hand to hand along a chain of handshakes, does each hand get less? How many handshakes until it is gone?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the fourth hand in the chain have as much glitter as the first? How many handshakes will it take before a hand has none? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same pinch of glitter and the same short handshake each time: one firm shake, for about one second. Count specks on the same part of each palm, inside a small paper square. Do the chain twice and compare.
results_table: Specks in the square, first try
Specks in the square, second try

materials.item: a small tube of glitter from a stationery shop, about one spoon. No glitter? Use a pinch of kumkum or rangoli colour instead.
a few drops of coconut oil or any cooking oil
a torch, or a phone torch
a piece of paper with a 2 cm square cut out of the middle, to count specks through
two or three people. Only two? Each person uses both hands, so the chain has four hands.
soap and water

experiments.safety: Keep glitter away from eyes and mouth. Wash hands with soap at the end. Wipe up spilt glitter with a damp cloth and put it in the dustbin.

schedule.what: Make a handshake chain. Count glitter specks on each hand, then do it again.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, then draw a bar for each hand in the chain, as tall as its number of specks.

flow.do: 1. Cut a 2 cm square hole in the middle of a piece of paper. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: The glitter will pass from hand to hand in a chain of handshakes. Will the last hand get as much as the first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Glitter will pass along a chain of handshakes. Will the last hand get as much? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Handshake Chain. Glitter passes along a line of handshakes, and you count how much reaches each hand.
flow.parent: With only two people, the four hands are: A's right (1), B's right (2), A's left (3), B's left (4). Each shake is between two different hands: 1 with 2, then 2 with 3, then 3 with 4.

flow.do: 1. Rub two drops of oil on the first hand. 2. Add one pinch of glitter. 3. Lay the paper on the palm and count the specks you see in the square, using the torch.
flow.say: Count the specks in the square on hand one. That is where the chain starts.
flow.kid: Count the specks in the square on hand one. Write the number.
flow.parent: There may be too many to count on the first hand. Write 'more than 50' and move on.

flow.do: 1. Hand one shakes hand two, once. 2. Hand two lays the paper square on its palm, and you count the specks with the torch and write the number. 3. Hand two shakes hand three, and hand three is counted the same way. 4. Hand three shakes hand four, and hand four is counted.
flow.say: One firm shake each, about one second. Count each hand straight after it has been shaken. What do you notice about the numbers?
flow.kid: Shake, then count. Shake the next hand, then count. Go all along the chain.
flow.parent: Expect the number to fall sharply at each shake, often to only a few specks by hand three or four. If two hands have the same number, that is fine: write what you see.

check.q: Which hand in the chain usually gets the least glitter?
check.why: Each shake passes on only part of the glitter, and keeps some on the hand that gave it. So less reaches each hand further down. Picking 'all the same' would mean the glitter makes more of itself as it goes. Glitter cannot do that, but some germs can, as you will see.

flow.do: 1. Everyone washes with soap. 2. Do the whole chain again. 3. Compare the two tries.
flow.say: Let's do it again. One try can be a fluke. Did the numbers fall the same way both times?
flow.kid: Wash. Do the chain again. Do the numbers fall the same way?

flow.do: Talk about what the results mean for real germs.
flow.say: Glitter got less at each hand. Germs often do too. But germs are alive. What could make them grow again further along the chain?
flow.kid: Glitter got less at each hand. Can germs grow again? Where?

ask.q: Where could germs multiply on their way?
good: In food that is left out warm.
Inside the next person's body.
In dirty water.

experiments.context: In this experiment you pass glitter along a chain of handshakes and count how much reaches each hand.

experiments.title: Warm or Cool: what happens to leftover rice?
experiments.question: Does cooked rice left out in a warm kitchen change faster than cooked rice kept in the fridge?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After two days, will the rice on the kitchen shelf look and smell different from the rice in the fridge? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use rice from the same pot, the same amount in each bowl, and the same kind of bowl and lid. Only the place changes: one bowl on a kitchen shelf, one in the fridge.
results_table: Rice on the shelf: smell from a distance
Rice in the fridge: smell from a distance

materials.item: 4 spoons of cooked rice from one pot, cooled
2 small steel bowls, the same size, each with a plate or lid
a strip of paper and a pencil for labels
a fridge

experiments.safety: Never taste the test rice. Smell it only by waving the air above the bowl towards your nose, and only with a grown-up. At the end, a grown-up throws the rice away in the dustbin or compost and washes the bowls with soap.

schedule.what: Put two spoons of cooked rice in each bowl, cover them, and put one on a shelf and one in the fridge. Draw how they look.
Look at both bowls and smell from a distance. Write what you notice.
Look and smell once more, talk about why the two bowls are different, and then a grown-up throws the rice away.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day, and draw both bowls side by side.

flow.do: 1. Put 2 spoons of rice in each bowl. 2. Cover both. 3. Label one 'shelf' and one 'fridge'. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: These two bowls of rice came from the same pot. One goes on the shelf, one in the fridge. What do you think they will look like in two days? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two bowls of rice. One on the shelf. One in the fridge. Guess what happens. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Warm or Cool, where you watch what happens to cooked rice kept warm and cool.

flow.do: Put one bowl on a kitchen shelf away from the stove, and one in the fridge. Draw both bowls.
flow.say: Draw them now, so we can compare later.
flow.kid: Put one bowl on the shelf, one in the fridge. Draw them both.

flow.do: On day 2, look at both bowls. Wave the air above each towards your nose.
flow.say: What do you see? What do you smell? Is the shelf rice different from the fridge rice?
flow.kid: Look at both bowls. Wave the air above each bowl towards your nose. Don't sniff close!
flow.parent: In a warm kitchen, the shelf rice often smells sour or feels sticky by day 2 or 3, and may show spots of mould by day 3. The fridge rice usually still looks and smells like rice. In a cool room the change may be slow or small: say so honestly, and look again on day 4.

flow.do: On day 3, two days after you started, look and smell once more. Talk about why the two bowls are different, then throw the rice away and wash the bowls.
flow.say: What do you think happened in the shelf bowl? Why did the fridge bowl change less?
flow.kid: Why did the shelf rice change? Why not the fridge rice?

ask.q: Why did the warm rice change faster?
good: Microbes multiplied in it, because it was warm and wet.
The fridge was too cold for them to grow fast.

flow.wait: Day 3: look and smell once more, then throw the rice away.

check.q: Why is it safer to put leftover sambar in the fridge soon after the meal?
options: Cold slows down the germs that multiply in warm food
Cold kills every germ at once
The fridge makes food taste better
check.why: In the cold, bacteria multiply very slowly, so they stay too few to make you ill. Picking 'kills every germ' is a common mistake. Most germs survive the fridge, and grow again when the food warms up. That is why food is heated well before eating.

experiments.context: In this experiment you keep cooked rice warm and cool for two days, and see where microbes multiply faster.

activities.title: How Many Hands? The door handle count

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil for tally marks
a sticky note to put by the main door

schedule.what: Guess, then count how many times the main door handle is touched in one evening.

activities.record: A tally chart with one row for each person, and one row for visitors such as the milk delivery or a neighbour.

flow.do: 1. Stick a note by the main door. 2. Ask your child to guess how many times the handle will be touched between 5 and 9 in the evening.
flow.say: Germs ride on things that many hands touch. Let's find out how many hands touch our door handle in one evening. Make a guess first. Why that number?
flow.kid: Guess how many times the door handle is touched this evening. Why?
flow.context: This is a short counting activity to start the unit. You find out how many hands touch one door handle in an evening.

flow.do: Through the evening, each person who touches the handle makes a tally mark on the note. Your child reminds everyone.
flow.say: Every time you touch the handle, put a mark on the note. Inside and outside both count.
flow.kid: Every touch, make a mark. Remind everyone, even the grown-ups!
flow.wait: Through the evening: count the touches.

flow.do: Add up the marks together.
flow.say: How many touches? How many different people? If one of them had cold germs on their hand, who else could the germs reach?
flow.kid: Add up the marks. How many people touched it?

ask.q: If one person had a cold, who else might the germs reach through this handle?
good: Everyone who touched it after them.
Even visitors, like the delivery person.

flow.think: What else in our home is touched by everyone?

activities.context: This is a counting activity. You find out how many hands touch your main door handle in one evening.

activities.title: One Germ Becomes Many: doubling with rice grains

materials.item: about 70 grains of raw rice, or dried moong
a steel plate
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Younger children may put grains in their nose or mouth, so watch them.

schedule.what: Put one grain on a plate. Then double the grains six times. Each doubling stands for 20 minutes of real time. Count and write each time.

activities.record: A table with two columns: 'Time' and 'Number of bacteria'. Draw the plate after the last doubling.

flow.do: Put one grain of rice on the plate.
flow.say: This grain is one bacterium in some warm rice. In the best conditions, some bacteria split into two about every 20 minutes. How many do you think there will be after 2 hours? Why?
flow.kid: One grain is one bacterium. Every 20 minutes, each bacterium splits into two. Guess: how many will there be after 2 hours?
flow.context: This activity shows how fast bacteria can multiply when they split in two again and again.

flow.do: 1. For each 20 minutes, put one new grain beside every grain already on the plate. 2. Write the time and the count each time.
flow.say: After 20 minutes, each grain gets a partner. How many are there now? After 40 minutes, double them again.
flow.kid: Each grain gets a partner. Count them. Write the number. Do it again.
flow.parent: The numbers go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. After 2 hours, which is 6 lots of 20 minutes, there are 64.

check.q: There are 16 bacteria. They all split in two. How many are there now?
check.why: Every one of the 16 becomes 2, so there are 16 + 16 = 32. Picking 17 or 18 means adding one or two new ones. But all of them split at once, so the number doubles.

flow.do: Look at the table together.
flow.say: After 2 hours there were 64. If the doubling carried on for 2 more hours, there would be more than 4,000. Why does warm food left out for hours worry doctors?
flow.kid: 64 after 2 hours! What about after 4 hours? Why does that matter?

ask.q: Why should leftover food go in the fridge soon?
good: So the bacteria can't double so many times.
Cold slows them down.

activities.context: This activity uses rice grains to show how fast one bacterium can become many by splitting in two.

activities.title: Be John Snow: find the bad well

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a ruler, to draw the map
a red pencil and a blue pencil

schedule.what: Mark where people fell ill on a made-up map, and find which well spread the illness.

activities.record: The map with a red dot for each ill family, and a circle round the well you think is to blame. Write one sentence on why.

flow.do: 1. Draw a grid of 6 squares across and 6 down, and number the rows and columns 1 to 6. 2. Draw well A in square 2 across, 2 down. 3. Draw well B in square 5 across, 5 down. 4. Draw well C in square 5 across, 1 down.
flow.say: This is a made-up colony with three wells. Families take water from the well closest to their house. Some families have fallen ill with loose motions.
flow.kid: Draw the map. Put in the three wells, A, B and C.
flow.context: This is a map puzzle, like the one John Snow solved in London in 1854. You mark where people fell ill and find which well spread the illness.

flow.do: 1. Squares are given as across, then down. 2. Mark a red dot for each ill family: 1-1, 2-1, 1-2, 2-2, 3-2, 1-3, 2-3, 3-3, 2-4 and 6-6. 3. Mark a blue dot for each family who stayed well: 4-1, 6-1, 6-2, 5-4, 4-5, 6-5, 5-6.
flow.say: Red dots are families who fell ill. Blue dots are families who stayed well. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Put red dots where families fell ill. Put blue dots where families stayed well. What do you see?

flow.do: Ask which well is to blame, and how the family at the red dot at 6-6 could have fallen ill.
flow.say: Most red dots are round well A. But one family at 6-6 is far from it, next to well B. How could that family have caught the illness?
flow.kid: Which well is to blame? What about the red dot far away?

ask.q: How could the family at 6-6 have fallen ill?
good: They went to well A anyway, maybe because they liked its water.
Someone brought water from well A to them.
They ate at a house near well A.

check.q: Nine ill families live round well A. One lives far away. Which well should be closed first?
options: Well A, because most ill families drink from it
Well B, because one ill family lives near it
All three, because illness is in the air
check.why: The ill families cluster round well A, so that is the best clue. The one far family can be checked by asking where they got their water. John Snow did exactly this. 'Illness is in the air' was the common idea in 1854, but bad air would not stay round one well.

flow.do: Read the 'How we found out' card about John Snow together.
flow.say: John Snow did this with real streets in London. One family far away turned out to have water brought from the bad pump.

constraints: Use only things from home: string, cardboard, tape, an old cloth, a hook.
It must not damage the door, and a grown-up must agree to it.
A child must be able to use it easily.
Any loop must be short and hang low, so it can never wrap round a neck.
materials: a wooden spoon or a hanger

Put a paper towel or small cloth by the tap to open the door with, and wash that cloth every day.
creative: Make a cardboard hook that slides over the handle and can be pushed down with an elbow.

items.p: Which of these is caused by a virus?
items.why: Colds are caused by viruses. Cholera is caused by bacteria, ringworm by a fungus, and a broken arm by no germ at all.

items.p: Most microbes are germs that make us ill.
items.why: False. Only a few kinds of microbe are germs. Your body carries trillions of bacteria, and nearly all of them do no harm.

items.p: Sort these ways germs travel into the right group.
items.why: Germs need a ride. Some ride on hands and the things hands touch, some on droplets in the air, some in water and food, and some on insects.

items.p: In the Glitter Trail, round 2 put the glitter on the carrier's elbow. What usually happened?
opts: Much less glitter reached the things and the other people
items.why: The elbow does not open doors or press buttons, so the glitter mostly stayed on it. That is why we cough into our elbow.

items.p: When germs get inside your body and multiply, that is called an ________.
items.why: An infection means germs have got in and are multiplying. Germs just sitting on your skin are not an infection.

items.p: Where do germs most often get into the body?
opts: Through the eyes, nose and mouth
Through dry skin with no cuts
items.why: The eyes, nose and mouth have soft, wet linings that germs can get through. Skin with no cuts keeps most germs out.

items.p: Match each habit to the link it breaks.
pairs: Keeps your germs away from others
items.why: Each habit breaks a different link in a germ chain. Breaking any one link stops that chain.

items.p: You can catch a cold from someone you never touched.
items.why: True. Germs can ride on things like buttons and handles, or in droplets in the air.

items.p: You have a cold. Which is the best way to sneeze?
items.why: An elbow catches most of the droplets, and does not touch handles or food. A hand catches them too, but then spreads them to everything it touches.

items.p: Put this germ chain in order.
items: Lakshmi eats a biscuit without washing
He does not wash after the toilet
a: He does not wash after the toilet
Lakshmi eats a biscuit without washing
items.why: The chain goes from the ill person, out on his hand, onto the handle, onto Lakshmi's hand, and into her mouth.

items.p: Draw a germ chain in your home with four links. Then draw a pair of scissors cutting one link.
items.a: Any chain with an ill person, a way out, a ride and a next person, with one link cut.
items.why: Drawing the chain shows that you know germs need a ride, and that one habit can break it.

items.p: Why should you wash your hands even on a day you feel well?
items.a: Because you can carry germs, and pass them on, before you feel ill, or without ever feeling ill.
items.why: Many germs spread before a person has symptoms. Washing every day breaks chains you cannot see.

items.p: Which of these is NOT contagious?
items.why: A broken leg cannot pass from one person to another. Chickenpox, colds and flu are caused by germs that spread.

items.p: Kavya has a cold. Her friend Nandini had a cold last week, but Kavya never sat near her.

views.says: Colds come from people breathing on you. Kavya must have sat next to someone else with a cold.
The cold came to me on the lift button. Nandini pressed it after wiping her nose, and then I pressed it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you saw in the Glitter Trail. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence: in the Glitter Trail, people who never touched the carrier still got glitter from the handle and remote. It also says what the other side has right: colds do spread through droplets in the air too, so both can happen.
items.why: Both ways are real. Scientists still argue about which matters more for colds, so a good answer uses evidence and does not throw the other view away.

items.p: Germs that travel through the air ride in tiny drops of spit and mucus called ________.
items.why: Coughs and sneezes spray droplets. They can carry germs to people and things nearby.

items.p: In the Handshake Chain, where glitter passed along four hands, the fourth hand usually had as many specks as the first.
items.why: False. Each shake passes on only part of the glitter and keeps some on the hand that gave it. So less reaches each hand down the chain.

items.p: In the Handshake Chain, each hand got less glitter than the hand before. Why might real germs not always get fewer along a chain?
opts: Some germs can multiply on the way, for example in warm food
items.why: Glitter cannot make more of itself, but bacteria can multiply in warm, wet places. So a few germs on a hand can become many in a plate of food left out.

items.p: Starting from 1 bacterium, the number doubles 6 times: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ____.
items.why: 32 doubled is 64. At each step, every bacterium splits into two, so the number doubles.

items.p: In Warm or Cool, one bowl of rice sat on a shelf and one in the fridge. Why did the shelf rice change faster?
opts: The fridge adds a special chemical
Light from the window spoiled it
items.why: Bacteria and moulds multiply much faster in warmth. Cold slows them down, though it does not kill them all.

items.p: Antibiotics are a good medicine for a cold.
items.why: False. Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work only on bacteria. Taking them when not needed helps bacteria learn to resist them.

items.p: Two children sit near an ill friend. Only one of them catches the cold. What is the best explanation?
opts: Fewer germs reached the other child, or their body cleared them
The other child was lucky, and germs have nothing to do with it
items.why: Whether you get ill depends on how many germs reach you, where they get in, and how ready your body is to fight. Picking 'germs have nothing to do with it' misses that the cold is caused by a virus.

items.p: Cold viruses can make copies only inside someone's nose or throat, and the body clears them out in about a week. Why does a sneeze help the viruses?
items.a: A sneeze carries copies of the virus out of one body, so they can reach a new nose before the first body clears them out.
items.why: Looking at it from the virus's side: without a way to reach a new body, that family of viruses comes to an end.

items.p: Dengue spreads through mosquito bites. Which habit breaks this chain best?
opts: Emptying standing water so mosquitoes cannot breed
items.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, such as in flower-pot trays and old tyres. Empty them, and fewer mosquitoes are born to carry the virus. Hand-washing does not stop a mosquito.

items.p: Is it caused by bacteria or a virus?
items.why: Cholera, typhoid and tuberculosis are caused by bacteria. Colds, chickenpox and flu are caused by viruses.

items.p: In the Glitter Trail, which thing in your home carried glitter to the most people? Why that one?
items.a: A strong answer names the thing, often the main door handle or the remote, and says it was touched by the most hands, so it picked up glitter from the carrier and passed it to everyone after.
items.why: Things touched by many hands are the busiest links in a germ chain.

items.p: A doctor finds that 9 of 10 ill families in a colony drink from the same well. The best clue is that the illness is in the ________.
items.why: When ill families cluster round one water source, that water is the best clue. John Snow used this clue in London in 1854.

items.p: Why can someone pass on flu before they know they are ill?
opts: The virus multiplies and leaves the body a day or so before symptoms start
Flu only spreads before you are ill
The fever makes the germs jump out
items.why: The virus is already multiplying in the nose and throat before the body's fight makes you feel ill. So some copies get out first.

items.p: Your building has one lift and 40 families. Why does a cough into a hand matter more there than in a house on its own?
items.a: Because the lift button is touched by people from all 40 families, so germs on one hand can reach many families through it.
items.why: The more hands share one thing, the further a germ can travel through that thing.

items.p: Which of these makes leftover sambar safest to eat the next day?
opts: Cover it, cool it, put it in the fridge within 2 hours, and heat it well before eating
Leave it on the stove overnight with the lid on
Leave it open so it cools faster
items.why: Cooling it quickly keeps bacteria from multiplying, the cover keeps flies off, and heating it well kills most germs that grew. Food safety advice is not to leave cooked food out for more than 2 hours.

items.p: A neighbour says, "Washing hands is a waste of time, because germs are everywhere anyway." What would you say back? Use what you know about chains.
items.a: A strong answer says that most microbes are harmless, and that the germs that matter travel along chains of hands and things. Washing breaks the way-in link, so fewer germs reach the mouth, nose or eyes.
items.why: Washing does not remove every microbe. It cuts the number of germs that get a ride to the next person, and that lowers the chance of illness.

items.p: John Snow found that workers at a brewery near the bad pump hardly ever got cholera. Why did that support his idea?
opts: They drank beer and the brewery's own water, not water from the pump
Beer kills every germ in the body
items.why: The workers breathed the same air as everyone nearby, but did not drink the pump water. So bad air could not be the cause, and the water could.
items.context: In 1854, John Snow studied a cholera outbreak in London. Most people who died lived near one water pump on Broad Street.

items.p: A widow far away in Hampstead died of cholera in the same week. Her family said she had Broad Street water brought to her, because she liked its taste. What did this show?
opts: The illness travelled with the water, not the air
Cholera can fly across a city
items.why: She lived far from the air around Broad Street, but she drank its water and caught cholera. The water was the link.
items.context: In 1854, John Snow studied a cholera outbreak in London. Most people who died lived near one water pump on Broad Street.

items.p: Draw a germ chain for an illness that travels in water: from a sick person, to dirty waste, to a well, to the people who drink from it. Then draw where you could break the chain.
items.a: A chain of pictures joined by arrows, with a break marked, for example at the well or the pump.
items.why: Drawing the chain shows how the illness travels in water, and that breaking one link, like closing a dirty well, protects everyone after it.

items.p: Scientists have argued for fifty years about how colds travel.

views.says: Colds spread mostly on hands. We found cold viruses on ill people's hands, and healthy people caught colds after touching those hands and then their eyes or nose.
Colds spread mostly through the air. Healthy men who could not touch their faces still caught colds from men they played cards with.
Both happen. Which matters more may depend on the place and the virus, so break both links.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing, and why? Then say what evidence would change your mind.
items.a: A strong answer uses the evidence from each test, notices that each test blocked a different path, and says what new test could decide it, such as blocking both paths in turn with the same people.
items.why: There is no single right answer yet. A good scientist weighs the evidence and says what would settle it.

items.p: A germ that makes people very ill very fast often spreads less than a cold does. Why?
items.a: Someone very ill stays in bed and meets few people, so the germ has few chances to reach a new body. A cold lets people go about their day, so it has many chances.
items.why: Germs go on only if their copies reach a new body. The fewer people the ill person meets, the fewer chances the germs have.

items.p: Bacteria double 3 times every hour. Starting with 1 bacterium, about how many are there after 3 hours?
items.why: 3 hours is 9 doublings. 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512. Picking 9 means counting doublings, not bacteria.

items.p: In the Glitter Trail, why did you check everyone's hands before you started?
items.a: To make sure nobody already had glitter, so any glitter we found later came from the carrier.
items.why: A fair test rules out other causes. Scientists checking where a germ came from do the same.

items.p: A town's cholera cases drop after the well is closed. But they were already falling before. What should a careful scientist say?
opts: The well may have caused the outbreak, but the drop alone does not prove it
The well was definitely not the cause
items.why: This really happened with the Broad Street pump. The outbreak was already slowing when the handle was removed. Snow's best evidence was where the ill people got their water, not the drop.

items.p: Glitter is a good pretend germ in one way, and a poor one in another. Say one of each.
items.a: Good: it rides on hands and things, like germs, and you can see it. Poor: it cannot multiply, and real germs can also die on dry surfaces.
items.why: A model helps us see something we cannot see. It is useful to know where the model is like the real thing and where it is not.

items.p: Why does a vaccine protect people who did not have it, as well as people who did?
opts: Vaccinated people break the chain, so the germ reaches fewer people
The vaccine spreads through the air
It makes the germ weaker everywhere
items.why: A vaccinated person rarely catches the germ, so they rarely pass the germ on. When most people are vaccinated, the germ runs out of links.

items.p: Draw or describe a germ chain that goes through water, from one family to another.
items.a: For example: an ill person's loose motions get into a well or a leaking pipe, and another family drinks that water without boiling it.
items.why: This is how cholera and typhoid spread. Toilets that keep waste away from water, and boiling or filtering, break this chain.

items.p: A scientist can gather evidence, such as a map of where people fell ill, to show others an idea she already thinks is right.
items.why: True. Scientists often have an idea first, then gather and show evidence so others can check it. John Snow drew his cholera map this way.

items.p: You wash your hands carefully all week, and your grandmother does not catch your cold. Why is it hard to be sure your care is what stopped her getting ill?
items.a: Because when a chain is broken, nobody falls ill, so there is nothing to see. You can only compare with times or places where the chain was not broken.
items.why: Scientists measure this by comparing many families or towns, some with a habit and some without.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether soap takes glitter off hands better than water alone. What stays the same? What changes?
items.a: A strong answer keeps the same amount of glitter, the same hand, the same rubbing time and the same water, and changes only soap or no soap. It counts the specks left after washing.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing at a time, so any difference can be put down to that one thing.

items.p: London's cholera outbreaks stopped after the city built sewers and cleaned its water. Why did that work better than telling each person to be careful?
opts: Clean water breaks the chain for everyone at once
Sewers kill the cholera bacteria in every person
items.why: Some links are too big for one person to break. A city can break them for everyone together.

quiz.p: Which of these is a germ?
opts: The virus that causes a cold
The bacteria that turn milk into curd
quiz.why: A germ is a microbe or virus that can make us ill, like the cold virus. Curd bacteria are helpful microbes. A mosquito is an insect that can carry germs, but is not a germ.

quiz.p: Which of these illnesses is caused by bacteria?
quiz.why: Cholera is caused by bacteria in dirty water. Colds and chickenpox are caused by viruses, which are much smaller and can only make copies inside cells.

quiz.p: Which of these can carry germs from one person to another?
quiz.why: Germs ride on handles, on tumblers and in cough droplets. Each is a different way, and all of them carry germs.

quiz.p: Dengue spreads from one person to another through what?
quiz.why: Dengue virus travels in the blood, carried from one person to the next by a mosquito. That is why emptying standing water helps.

quiz.p: A girl has glitter on her hand and touches the door handle. Her grandmother never touches her, but opens the door. What will the grandmother's hand have?
opts: No glitter, because she never touched the girl
quiz.why: The glitter rides from the girl's hand to the handle, then to her grandmother's hand. Picking 'no glitter' means thinking germs pass only by touching people.

opts: Germs getting inside the body and multiplying
Germs sitting on a door handle
quiz.why: An infection means germs are inside you and growing in number. Germs on a handle have not infected anyone yet.

quiz.p: Some bacteria can split in two every 20 minutes. Starting with 1, how many are there after one hour?
quiz.why: One hour is three lots of 20 minutes, so they double three times: 1, 2, 4, 8. Picking 3 counts the splits, not the bacteria.

quiz.p: You have just come home from the park. When is the most important time to wash your hands?
quiz.why: Washing before eating breaks the link from your hand to your mouth. Washing later is still good, but the germs could already be in.

quiz.p: You have flu. What is the best way to protect your classmates?
opts: Stay home until you are well
Go to school and sit at the back
Go to school and take medicine
quiz.why: Staying home breaks the very first link, so your germs never reach the classroom. Sitting at the back still shares the air, the door handle and the tap.

quiz.p: Long ago, many people thought bad-smelling air caused cholera. Which finding would show that dirty water, not air, was the cause?
opts: People who breathed the same air but drank clean water did not fall ill
The air near the river smelled bad
Mosquitoes were seen near the houses
quiz.why: If air were the cause, everyone breathing it would fall ill. If only those who drank the dirty water fell ill, the water is to blame. Mosquitoes spread other illnesses, like malaria, not cholera.

quiz.p: Many people near one water pump fall ill. How could you find out whether the pump is to blame?
opts: Ask each family where they get their water, and see whether most who fell ill drank from that pump
Look for the germ with your own eyes
quiz.why: Comparing who drank the water with who fell ill shows the link. Germs are too small to see with your eyes. John Snow did this in London in 1854.

applications: Doctors and health workers trace outbreaks the way John Snow did, by asking where ill people ate, drank and went.
Hospitals have rules for hand-washing and hand rubs between patients.
Cities treat drinking water with chlorine and filters so that cholera and typhoid cannot spread through the taps.
Food stalls and hotel kitchens follow food safety rules, such as keeping cooked food hot or cold.
Schools send children with chickenpox or conjunctivitis home until they are better.
Health workers spray and empty standing water to stop mosquitoes that carry dengue and malaria.
Vaccines stop germs such as measles and polio from passing along chains of people.
Many schools teach children to cough into the elbow and to cover the mouth.

open_questions.q: Which way do colds spread most: on hands or through the air?
open_questions.why_open: Careful studies have found different answers. It may depend on the virus, the place and how close people are.

open_questions.q: Why do some people carry a germ and stay well, while others get very ill from the same germ?
open_questions.why_open: Genes, past infections, age and the microbes already in the body all seem to matter, but nobody can yet predict it for one person.

open_questions.q: Where will the next new germ come from?
open_questions.why_open: Many new germs jump to people from animals, such as bats, birds and pigs. Scientists watch for them, but cannot yet say which one or when.
Viruses make copies of themselves and change over time, but only inside cells. Scientists still argue about where to draw the line.

open_questions.q: Can we stop bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics?
open_questions.why_open: Bacteria change quickly. Doctors are trying to use fewer antibiotics and find new ones, but nobody knows if we will keep ahead.

maths.problem: In the door handle count, a family touched the handle 18 times between 5 and 9 in the evening. That is 4 hours. About how many touches is that each hour?
maths.explain: 18 touches in 4 hours. 4 times 4 is 16 and 4 times 5 is 20. 18 is between them, so about 4 or 5 touches an hour.
maths.context: In the door handle count, everyone makes a tally mark each time they touch the main door handle in one evening.
maths.why_maths: Sharing the total between the hours shows how often a germ on the handle would get a new ride.

maths.problem: Some bacteria can split in two every 20 minutes in warm food. Starting with 1, how many are there after 2 hours?
maths.explain: 2 hours is 6 lots of 20 minutes, so the bacteria double 6 times. 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.
maths.context: In One Germ Becomes Many, one grain of rice stands for one bacterium, and you double the grains for every 20 minutes.
maths.why_maths: Doubling shows why a few germs in food can become many very quickly, and why time out of the fridge matters.

maths.problem: A class has 30 children. One child comes to school with a cold and passes it to 2 friends. Each of them passes it to 2 more the next week. How many children have caught the cold by the end of the second week, including the first child?
maths.explain: The first child is 1. In week 1, 2 more catch it, so 3. In week 2, each of those 2 passes it to 2 more, which is 4. 3 + 4 = 7.
maths.context: This is about how a cold spreads through a class when each ill child passes it to two others.
maths.why_maths: Adding up each step shows how a chain branches out and gets bigger every week.

maths.problem: In the Handshake Chain, there were 48 specks on hand 1, 12 on hand 2 and 3 on hand 3. What pattern do you see? How many would you expect on hand 4?
maths.answer: Each hand had about a quarter of the hand before. So hand 4 would have about 1 speck, or none.
maths.explain: 48 divided by 4 is 12, and 12 divided by 4 is 3. So each shake passed on about a quarter. 3 divided by 4 is less than 1, so hand 4 would have 1 speck or none.
maths.context: In the Handshake Chain, glitter passes along a line of handshakes, and you count the specks on each hand.
maths.why_maths: Spotting a pattern in the numbers lets you predict the next hand before you count it.

maths.problem: John Snow wrote that a brewery near the bad pump had about 70 workers, and none of them died of cholera. A workhouse nearby had 535 people living in it, and its own well. Only 5 of them died. Why are these numbers good evidence against bad air?
maths.answer: Both groups breathed the same air as their neighbours, who were dying in large numbers. But they did not drink the pump water, and almost none of them died.
maths.explain: If bad air caused cholera, about as many brewery workers and workhouse people should have died as people in the houses around them. 0 out of 70 and 5 out of 535 are far fewer, so the air was not the cause.
maths.context: In 1854, John Snow studied a cholera outbreak in London. Most people who died lived near one water pump on Broad Street.
maths.why_maths: Comparing groups that differ in only one way, here the water they drank, tells you what caused the difference.
