roots.context: We have followed glitter from hand to handle to hand, and seen how germs travel along chains. Now we ask what these chains tell us about ourselves and the people around us.

deep_truth.truth: In the Glitter Trail experiment, one person, the carrier, has glitter on their hand. People who never touched the carrier still got glitter on their hands. It rode there on the door handle and the remote. Germs travel the same way, from hand to thing to hand. So your health is joined to people you may never meet.
deep_truth.habit: We think of catching an illness as something between us and the one ill person beside us. Often the germ came along a longer chain, through handles, buttons, water and air shared by many people.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Glitter Trail, the helper never went near the carrier, yet had glitter on the palms from the handle and the remote. John Snow found a widow in Hampstead who died of cholera from Broad Street water carried to her across London.

three.who_am_i: You are one link in many chains. What your hands touch reaches people you will never see.
three.what_is_life: Germs go on only if their copies reach a new body. Every living being has to find a way to keep their family going.
three.what_is_this_world: A building, a street and a city share handles, buttons, water and air. The world is joined by what we touch in common.

roots.thread: Germs on one hand can travel through a whole building, because many people touch the same few things. In the same way, one habit in one person, like coughing into an elbow, breaks every chain that would have passed through them. So the care one family takes protects the other families who touch the same handles. A home is not closed off from its neighbours, even when its door is shut.

teachings.teaching: An old Indian book on surgery says that some diseases pass from person to person. They spread by touching bodies, by breath, by eating together, by sitting and lying together, and by sharing clothes, garlands and ointments. Fever and eye infections are among the diseases it names.
teachings.link: Two thousand years ago, Indian doctors had already noticed that illness can travel through shared things, such as clothes and garlands, and not only from person to person. The Glitter Trail shows the same thing.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: The god Indra has a net that stretches in every direction. At every knot hangs a jewel, and each jewel reflects all the others. Nothing in the net stands alone.
teachings.link: In a building of flats, every family's hands meet on the same lift button and door handles. What is on one family's hands ends up on the others' hands, the way each jewel reflects all the others.

science.text: Germs spread along chains of contact, through people, shared things, droplets, water, food and insects. Breaking links stops outbreaks.
How much each path matters for colds and flu, hands or air, is still argued about.

other_view.who: Many doctors and public health workers
other_view.view: The biggest causes of germ spread are not single hands but dirty water, crowded homes, poor toilets and lack of health care. Telling families to wash their hands matters less than giving every family clean water and a toilet, which is the job of governments.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1854, cholera broke out in Soho, in London. More than 500 people died in about ten days. Most doctors believed cholera came from miasma, bad-smelling air from rubbish and sewers. A doctor called John Snow thought it came from dirty water. He went from house to house, asking where each family got their water. Nearly all the dead had drunk from one street pump, on Broad Street. Two groups nearby breathed the same air but did not use the pump: about 70 workers at a brewery, who drank beer and the brewery's own water, and 535 people in a workhouse with its own well. None of the brewery workers died, and only 5 people in the workhouse did. A widow far away in Hampstead also died. She liked the taste of the Broad Street water, so her family brought it to her. On 8 September 1854, the pump's handle was removed. A local priest, Henry Whitehead, at first wanted to prove Snow wrong. Instead, he found how the outbreak probably started: a sick baby's nappies had been washed into a cesspit next to the well.
how_we_found_out.who: John Snow, a doctor in London, and Henry Whitehead, a priest in Soho
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most doctors thought cholera came from miasma, bad-smelling air. Snow showed that people who breathed the same air but drank other water stayed well, while a woman far away who drank the pump water died.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home in a city flat with the materials listed. The Glitter Trail needs only one other person: the carrier touches a fixed list of things, the helper uses them after, and everyone's hands are checked with a torch before and after. The Handshake Chain counts specks through a 2 cm square straight after each shake, and works with two people. The rice test is never tasted and is smelled only from a distance; in a warm kitchen the shelf rice often smells sour by day 2 or 3, and in a cool room the change may be small. Every card in the games is written out, and the Germ Chain cards each have a STOP card that fits.
